en.html:
At that one roar, the boy and the three warriors who appeared to be his guards literally jumped. Swept along, perhaps, by the pressure of the voice, they hurried past me in a fluster.

All that time, I could not move.
Certainly I had no reason to stop them. But even if I had, breaking free of the murderous intent binding me from the front would likely have been impossible.


The four sets of footsteps vanished far behind me.

We faced one another in <ruby>mutual<rt>mutual</rt></ruby> high guards. Each held the enemy within range of a downward cut.

Shishiku Ootori's point sat somewhat higher. Against my more reclined blade, that exposed its length, a disadvantage; in exchange, his cut would arrive sooner.

Utter stillness. Like a dead tree standing alone in a field, Shishiku Ootori remained <ruby>still<rt>still</rt></ruby>.

en.html:
My assessment of the opponent required correction.
Not a battlefield <ruby>champion<rt>vanguard</rt></ruby>, wielding a mighty sword in the full confidence of overwhelming his enemy—rather, he seemed to possess the mind and skill of a <ruby>swordsman<rt>swordmaster</rt></ruby>.

Whether that was his natural <ruby>swordsmanship<rt>style</rt></ruby> was another question. For the present contest, its suitability had to be acknowledged. We were on the ground, and indoors at that, in <ruby>cramped<rt>cramped</rt></ruby> quarters.

Forget wings soaring through the sky; even adamantine strength could scarcely be used to its full extent. For armored swordplay that <ruby>relied<rt>relied</rt></ruby> upon strength and speed, this was a particularly disagreeable situation.
Here, subtle technique would do the deciding.

If the enemy had that stored beneath his steel and was waiting for me, a careless advance or retreat was out of the question. Charge in without thought, and the returning stroke would have me vomiting blood.

Check <ruby>my side's<rt>my</rt></ruby> attack at its inception—or let me strike, deflect, then cut me thoroughly down once my balance broke. Either way, that single exchange would settle the contest.

I too would have to enter it with a technique prepared.

俺は対手への評価を修正する必要に迫られた。
　敵を呑んで掛かる意気に満ちて剛剣を扱う、戦場の
<ruby>猛将<rt>バンガード</rt></ruby>ではなく――むしろ<ruby>剣術使い<rt>ソードマスター</rt></ruby>の心技を備えている
と見られる。

　それが彼本来の<ruby>剣質<rt>スタイル</rt></ruby>なのかどうかは置き、今この場
の争闘において適性である事は認めねばならなかった。
　地上、しかも<ruby>狭隘<rt>きょうあい</rt></ruby>な屋内である。

　天空を翔ける翼はおろか、金剛力も充分には発揮し
難い。力と速度を<ruby>恃<rt>たの</rt></ruby>む武者刀法が特に苦手とする局面
であった。
　このような場では精妙な術技こそが物を言う。

　敵騎がそれを甲鉄の下に蓄えて俺を待っているなら
ば、間違っても迂闊な進退はできなかった。
　無思慮に斬り込みなどした途端、切り返しの一太刀
を食って血反吐を吐く。

　<ruby>我方<rt>こちら</rt></ruby>の打つ出端を制するか――打ち込ませておいて
受け流し、体勢の崩れたところを存分に斬り下げるか。
　いずれにせよ、勝負はその一合で終わるだろう。

　こちらも術を仕込んで臨まねばならない。

en.html:
The opponent remained motionless. The attacking spirit I sent out passed him like wind through a willow.

In other words, he <ruby>had not been deceived<rt>・・・・・・・</rt></ruby>.
Had the enemy taken my obvious aggression for an opportunity and rushed to strike me first, my fully prepared <ruby>returning technique<rt>counter</rt></ruby> could have stripped him of the power to fight in one stroke.

Even if he intended to let me attack and then answer, I should have been able to unsettle him by remaining contrary to expectation, never delivering the blow however long he waited.

<ruby>Yet<rt>Yet</rt></ruby> the enemy showed no response at all. His posture never wavered; his sword's menace remained solemnly composed.

He had seen entirely through my <ruby>luring technique<rt>feint</rt></ruby>.

I could not suppress a quiet click of the tongue. The failure itself was one thing; what it had told the enemy was another. He must have understood now... I also had techniques ready for use.

He would grow more cautious, make his methods deeper and subtler. A difficult opponent, made more difficult by my own efforts.

Should I have done nothing rash, simply maintained my guard <ruby>still<rt>still</rt></ruby> and waited for his impatience...?

An excellent question, now that its answer could serve no purpose.

There was no time to lose heart. He would move cautiously, yes, but cautiously was not necessarily <ruby>the same as<rt>equal to</rt></ruby> slowly.
Once his plan was settled, he could attack this very instant. Let my attention wander and I would not answer it. A small failure needed to be forgotten quickly.

He was coming————
He would come.

If that silent exchange had tipped the balance even slightly in his favor, he would not discard the opportunity. Until the balance returned—until I recovered my mind and body and prepared another tactic—he had no obligation to wait for me.

He was coming.
But in what form...

慮って、俺は密やかな舌打ちを禁じ得なかった。
　今ので、敵は察した筈だ……こちらにも術を用いる
用意があるという事実を。

　益々慎重になり、技は深く巧妙なるを期すだろう。
　難敵が余計に難敵と化す。

　下手に仕掛けず、<ruby>凝<rt>じつ</rt></ruby>と構え続け、敵手の焦燥を待つ
べきだったか……？

　そう思っても、今となっては詮ない。

　挫けている場合ではなかった。
　敵は慎重に動くであろうが、それは時間を掛けると
いう事と必ずしも<ruby>同義<rt>イコール</rt></ruby>ではないのだ。

　策を決すれば、この刹那にも仕掛けて来る。
　心気を迷妄させていては対応できない。小さな失敗
などさっさと忘れるべきだった。

　敵は来る――――
　来るだろう。

　今の音なき攻防で勝負の天秤がやや己の側に傾いた
と見たなら、その機を捨て去る筈はない。
　天秤が再び平衡に戻るまで――俺が心身を立て直し
再び術策を講ずるまで、待ってやる義理などないのだ。

　敵は来る。
　が、それが如何なる形を取るか……

All Shishiku had done was lower his sword from the high guard. That alone. So that the point faced his opponent—me.
The enemy sword's guard, its point, and my eyes lay on <ruby>one straight line<rt>・・・</rt></ruby>.

The opponent's cool eyes watched every movement I made.
He was waiting—for me to undo myself.
Would I exhaust mind and body until my legs weakened? Or launch a desperate attack? Whichever I chose, there was no chance of winning.
Unless, in this state, I possessed the mental strength to keep my ordinary composure to the end—but—
